statement: Social Security still changes the legal name on your Social Security record. A valid court order for a name change is one of the events Social Security recognizes as changing your legal name, and you apply with Form SS-5, the Application for a Social Security Card.
detail: Social Security's policy manual defines your legal name as your first name and last name — the name you use to sign legal documents. For a person born in the United States, that is generally the name shown on the birth certificate, unless the name changed through an event such as a marriage or a valid court order for a name change. The sex marker on your record is handled separately and under a different rule — see the Social Security sex marker step.

source.title: SSA Program Operations Manual System (POMS) RM 10212.001 — Defining the Legal Name for an SSN

statement: Social Security does not update the sex marker on your Social Security record to match your gender identity. Its policy manual says the agency is only correcting or changing the sex field on the Numident to reflect the number holder's sex at birth.
detail: As evidence of sex, Social Security asks for a birth certificate established by a state or local bureau of vital statistics that reflects sex at birth, or the sex recorded through enumeration at birth; if you were born abroad, a foreign birth certificate or a Consular Report of Birth Abroad that lists sex at birth. This reverses Social Security's earlier practice of accepting a self-identified sex designation, and the underlying federal policy is being litigated, so confirm it against the official source before you rely on it. Your legal name is a separate matter and Social Security still processes a legal name change.

source.title: SSA Program Operations Manual System (POMS) RM 10212.200 — Changing NUMIDENT Data for Reasons Other than Name Change

statement: To update the name on your U.S. passport, submit a passport application with an original or certified copy of the document that legally changed your name, such as a court order.
detail: If your name changed within 1 year of your most recent passport being issued, mail Form DS-5504 with the name-change document — you will not have to submit any fees for this service. If it has been more than a year, renew by mail with Form DS-82 and a certified name-change document, or apply in person with Form DS-11. If you have no legal documentation of the change, you apply in person with Form DS-11 plus Form DS-60, Affidavit Regarding a Change of Name.

cost.note: No fee when you use Form DS-5504 within a year of issuance ($60 if you want it expedited). Otherwise standard application fees apply.

source.title: U.S. Department of State — Change or Correct a Passport

statement: The U.S. Department of State says it only issues a passport with an M or F sex marker that matches your biological sex at birth. It no longer issues U.S. passports or Consular Reports of Birth Abroad with an X marker.
detail: The Department points to Executive Order 14168, issued January 20, 2025. On November 6, 2025, the U.S. Supreme Court stayed the preliminary injunction that had been issued in June 2025, so the Department is only issuing passports that reflect sex at birth. Passports already issued stay valid until they expire, are replaced by the applicant, or are invalidated under federal regulations. This is under active litigation and can change — read the official page before you apply.

source.title: U.S. Department of State — Sex Markers in Passports
